value.overview: The Swallow-tailed Gull (Creagrus furcatus) is a distinctive tropical seabird of the eastern equatorial Pacific. It is the only species in its genus and spends most of its life over open ocean. The species is best known from breeding colonies on the Galápagos Islands and Malpelo Island, where adults forage mainly at night. Its deeply forked tail, dark head in breeding adults, and red orbital ring make it one of the most recognizable gulls in its range.
value.classification: The Swallow-tailed Gull belongs to the order Charadriiformes and family Laridae. It is the sole species in the genus Creagrus.
value.identification: Adults have a pale gray back and wings, a white body, and a strongly forked white tail. In breeding plumage, the head is black, contrasting with a white collar and body. The bill is black with a pale or whitish tip, the orbital ring is red, and the legs are pink. Nonbreeding adults have a largely white head with dark markings around the eyes. Juveniles are browner and more heavily mottled, with a less sharply defined tail pattern.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds mainly on rocky shores, cliffs, and small coastal islets of the Galápagos Islands and Malpelo Island. Outside the breeding colonies it disperses widely over the eastern Pacific, where it is usually found over deep ocean waters rather than inland habitats. In Costa Rica it is a rare but apparently regular visitor to Pacific waters, including the area around Isla del Coco and waters near the mainland coast. Records have been concentrated offshore, especially between late March and early May.
value.migrationStatus: It is not considered a conventional long-distance migrant. After breeding, individuals disperse widely through the eastern Pacific. In Costa Rica it occurs as a rare pelagic visitor, with repeated records indicating regular seasonal presence rather than year-round residence or local breeding.
value.breeding: Swallow-tailed Gulls breed colonially on bare rocky ground, cliffs, and ledges of oceanic islands. The main breeding populations are in the Galápagos and on Malpelo. Pairs generally produce a single egg, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the chick. Breeding is closely tied to marine food availability, and colonies may contain birds at different stages because reproduction can occur throughout much of the year. Chicks are fed regurgitated marine prey.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of fish, squid, and other marine animals. Swallow-tailed Gulls are especially notable for feeding at night, when they may capture squid and fish near the ocean surface. They also take prey associated with schools of fish, marine predators, or feeding activity around boats. Their long wings and maneuverable flight allow them to search broad areas of open water.
value.behavior: This gull spends much of its time flying over the open ocean and commonly rests on rocky islands or vessels. It is strongly nocturnal when foraging, an unusual adaptation among gulls. Adults are social around breeding colonies but may travel widely while feeding. Birds in Costa Rican waters have been observed near ships, and artificial lights may help attract them close to vessels at night.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established. Available information does not demonstrate a confirmed, sustained decline that would warrant a higher threat category.
